claims.text: Increasing the concentration of a nano-twin-promoting alloying element will increase nano-twin formation during deformation.
Increased nano-twin formation will improve toughness retention under demanding mechanical conditions.
The initial material is an equiatomic high-entropy alloy with a microstructure typical of standard processing.
The proposed intervention is an approximately 5 at% incremental increase in an unspecified nano-twin-promoting element.
High-strain-rate deformation at room temperature activates nano-twin formation in the proposed alloy.
The chemical modification will increase the density of newly formed deformation nano-twins.
The elevated concentration of the selected element chemically drives nano-twin formation during plastic deformation.
Impeded dislocation motion and crack propagation preserve or enhance toughness during severe deformation.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have a measurable increase in nano-twin density.
The increase in nano-twin density will correlate with higher fracture toughness.
The modification will improve strain-hardening behavior, which will contribute to toughness retention.
The equiatomic baseline has lower nano-twin density and associated toughness than the proposed modified alloy under identical test conditions.
The proposed behavior is expected near equiatomic composition, at moderate temperatures, and under deformation conditions favoring nano-twin activation.
The mechanism may fail at ultralow temperatures or when excessive chemical modification induces undesirable phases.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified alloy fails to show both a statistically significant increase in nano-twin density and a corresponding toughness improvement relative to the baseline.
